newsitem.title: CYPRUS: UK's Rifkind to talk peace to Cyprus leaders.
newsitem.headline: UK's Rifkind to talk peace to Cyprus leaders.

text.p: British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind will urge leaders of the Greek and Turkish Cypriots at separate meetings on Monday to bury their decades-old hostility and start peace talks.

Rifkind, the first British foreign secretary to visit the divided eastern Mediterranean island for more than 30 years, argues that the world wants to see an end to a conflict that it regards as a throwback to an earlier age.

"At a time when the Cold War is over, the Berlin Wall has fallen and apartheid is no more, surely it is not unrealistic that this small beautiful island can find a peace and justice acceptable to all," he told reporters on arrival in Cyprus.

Rifkind got an insight into the passions dividing the two communities when a small group of elderly Greek Cypriot women begged him for help on Sunday to find relatives missing since Turkish troops occupied the northern third of the island in 1974.

"The international community does not regard the status quo as tenable. Events of the last year have shown how fragile that status quo is," said a British official, referring to violence in which four people have been killed over the past six months in or near the U.N.-patrolled buffer zone splitting Cyprus.
Rifkind will first meet Cypriot President Glafcos Clerides before crossing the Green Line dividing Nicosia to hold talks with Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash.
"What he's trying to do is create an atmosphere of sufficient confidence to ensure face-to-face talks start as soon as possible next year," said one British official.
The Turkish Cypriots declared an independent state in 1983 but it is recognised only by Turkey. Cyprus was a British colony from 1914 until independence in 1960.
Rifkind, aware that the United Nations has nothing to show for decades of attempts to broker peace, was at pains to stress that any progress would be slow.

U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali said last week that the situation on Cyprus was the worst since the 1974 Turkish invasion after a coup engineered by the military regime then ruling Greece.
British officials said one leverage point that Rifkind might use would be the talks that Cyprus is due to start on becoming member of the European Union.
"We want to use the accession talks to give momentum to a political process which has been quiet for too long," one said.

The Cyprus membership talks, set to start six months after the EU completes its inter-governmental conference on reforming the 15-nation bloc, could begin in 1998 and Rifkind stressed the economic benefits for all the islanders.

"If the island remains divided, the accession talks will be complicated, more complicated than they would be at the end of a political process in Cyprus," one official said, noting it had taken Spain and Portugal six years to gain entry to the EU.
"I don't think the Cyprus problem can be solved by outside pressure from various countries," the official said. "But the EU accession timetable creates a sort of pressure on its own."
